outputs.notable: It misquotes the error and then reasons from its own paraphrase. The stack says "Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'map')", but X writes "**Actual:** TypeError — undefined is not an array, .map() called on undefined" and later builds an inference on that invented wording: "The error is specifically 'undefined is not an array,' not 'undefined has no property lines' — this suggests the whole data object might sometimes be undefined, not just a property." That distinction is manufactured; the real message does not support it. Second error: hypothesis 1 is ranked HIGH confidence on a mechanism that does not exist as described - an RSC payload carries its data serialized with the tree, so "hydration on the client doesn't happen in the order renderInvoiceLines expects" is not how a server component delivers props. Third: the hypothesis-5 probe ("Hard refresh the page ... and test again. Check if the error goes away") cannot discriminate anything against a 3% failure rate, so it is labelled a probe while being incapable of killing the hypothesis.

methodology_notes:
Three calls in this set could reasonably have gone the other way, and I want them on the record.

(1) Item 2 for OUTPUT W. The checklist asks the output to decline to invent a reproduction "and say so". W says so only by restating the given - a bolded header "**No reproduction steps known**" and "Since you can't manually reproduce it" - which is closer to echoing the user than to an act of restraint. I credited it because the behaviour the item is testing for is the absence of fabricated steps plus explicitness that none exist, and W has both. A judge holding out for a first-person refusal would mark W absent here, and I would not argue hard. X and Z state it as a blocker in their own voice, which is stronger. Y fails on any reading - it never raises the subject.

(2) Item 5 for OUTPUT X. X never writes `?? []` or `|| []`, so on a literal reading of the item's conditional clause it has nothing to warn about. But its hypothesis-1 probe contains `if (!Array.isArray(invoiceData?.lines)) { console.error(...); return null; // or fallback UI }`, which is the same swallowing behaviour wearing a diagnostic hat, and no part of the output tells the reader that rendering nothing where line items belong is a billing hazard. I scored it absent on the substance of the item rather than the letter. A judge who reads the snippet as pure instrumentation - it does log loudly before returning - would mark it present. This was my least confident call in the set.

(3) Item 4 for OUTPUT Z. Z is the only output containing both halves of the required distinction, but they are not welded together in one sentence: the trigger label sits in the Failure block, and the code-assumption cause sits inside hypothesis 2 of five. Worse, its verdict section states a root cause that contradicts hypothesis 2 - "The root cause is that the data is arriving undefined when it shouldn't be" locates the defect in the data, not in the code's assumption about it. I credited it because both statements are explicit and both are carried into the "Hypothesis 1 + 2 together" verdict, but a judge demanding one clean trigger-versus-root-cause sentence would mark it absent and the contradiction gives them a fair basis.

Two notes on how I applied the rules generally. Item 1 came out absent for all four, and I want to be clear that this is not a tie produced by fatigue: I searched each output for provenance language and found that all four state the 3%, the Thursday and the refactor as findings, with Z additionally converting the date into a specific and incorrect one. Item 3's "rough cost" requirement I read as satisfied by an ordinal label (CHEAP / MEDIUM / HIGHER), not requiring wall-clock or dollar estimates; if the intent was a quantified cost, X and Z would both fail and no output would pass item 3.

Finally, a limit on this scoring that the checklist does not cover: three of the four rank a client-renders-before-the-promise-resolves race as their leading theory, which is a doubtful mechanism for a React server component, since the payload carries its data with the tree. Item 3 rewards the form of ranked hypotheses with probes, and both X and Z earn it while leading with that mechanism. A high score here is evidence of good debugging discipline, not of a correct diagnosis.
